claim: Puter is licensed AGPL-3.0-only (package.json license field; LICENSE.txt is GNU AGPL v3; README says the whole repository is AGPL-3.0 unless stated otherwise)
Self-hosting Puter requires Docker with the compose plugin and a domain with a wildcard DNS record, because Puter routes by subdomain (api., site., app.)

The self-hosted stack is seven containers: Caddy, Valkey, MariaDB, DynamoDB-local, RustFS (S3), a bucket-init job and Puter itself; Ollama is optional; the header tells production users to "move state-bearing volumes to a backed-up location" (no built-in backup)
The compose file runs ghcr.io/heyputer/puter:main with pull_policy: always, and dynamodb-local and ollama on :latest, so a self-hosted install has no pinned version
Documented update procedure is docker compose pull then up -d; migrations re-apply idempotently; no rollback or pre-update backup step is documented
Local AI is an optional Ollama container behind the compose profile "ai", CPU-only unless a commented-out NVIDIA block is enabled; default model tinyllama (1.1B)
The AI chat driver ships provider adapters for about 20 providers, including claude, openai, gemini, mistral, deepseek, xai, openrouter, together, groq and ollama
Puter.js "User-Pays Model": each end user signs in with a Puter account that pays for that user's AI, storage and other usage; every user gets a free monthly allowance, then upgrades

Puter's MCP connector runs on Cloudflare Workers and lets an MCP client drive the caller's Puter filesystem and site hosting with the caller's Puter token or OAuth; tools include fs_write_file and fs_delete (recursive by default)
Backend is layered (controllers, drivers, services, stores, clients, config) with an extensions mechanism; the doc itself says metering and appTelemetry "should probably be core"
Hosted puter.com pricing (USD/month): Free 0 with 25 MB storage, Basic 10, Plus 25, Pro 100; "every paid plan unlocks every app"

Sandstorm is licensed Apache-2.0; the Sandstorm name and logo are trademarks
The installer refuses to run on anything but x86_64 ("Sorry, the Sandstorm server currently only runs on x86_64 machines")
Sandstorm needs unprivileged user namespaces; since v0.309 the installer adds an AppArmor profile on hosts that restrict them by default, such as Ubuntu 24.04
Self-update: polls install.sandstorm.io/<channel>, downloads the new bundle, verifies a detached GPG signature against the bundled release keyring and aborts the update if the check fails
Each update unpacks into a new versioned directory and atomically repoints a "latest" symlink; cleanupOldVersions then deletes older builds, so no previous build is kept for rollback

v0.309 (2026-10-08) is "the first community release": release signing key now held by three maintainers, Meteor 2.16 and MongoDB 7.0 with a database migration that "must be run manually"; v0.310 (2026-10-12) has no changes and tests the auto-update path
The previous release, v0.308, was dated 2023-08-06, about 26 months before v0.309; v0.307 notes releases moved from monthly to "as-needed"
Apps ship as signed .spk packages; "spk verify" checks the signature and prints the app ID, which is derived from the app's public key, and the package manifest is a Cap'n Proto struct

Every "grain" (one document, chat room and so on) runs in its own sandbox; the supervisor installs a seccomp-BPF syscall filter; the website says a grain cannot talk to the world without express permission
The Powerbox is the Sandstorm UI through which a user connects one app to another (a capability grant) instead of apps reaching each other directly
Sandstorm Oasis, the paid hosting service, began winding down on 2019-12-31; the app market and automatic updates for self-hosted servers continued
sandstorm.io now says it is "historical, from when Sandstorm was a startup" and that the open-source project moved to sandstorm.org, built by a community of volunteers

Sandstorm has a per-grain backup and restore tool (writes a grain plus its metadata to a zip, or restores one)
FreedomBox Service (Plinth) is distributed under the GNU AGPL version 3 or later; per-file licences are in debian/copyright
FreedomBox is "an official part of Debian" and is supported by the non-profit FreedomBox Foundation; it describes itself as a private server for non-experts
Latest package version at the pinned commit is freedombox 26.15, dated 2026-11-02, uploaded to Debian unstable
A FreedomBox app is a Python module (an App subclass) that declares the Debian packages it installs, for example the Kiwix app installs kiwix-tools
Updates use Debian unattended-upgrades plus needrestart; FreedomBox also checks hourly and can run an automatic dist-upgrade to the next Debian stable release
Before a dist-upgrade FreedomBox takes a snapper snapshot ("before dist-upgrade") if snapshots are supported, and pauses per-apt snapshots during the upgrade
Snapshots work only when the root file system is btrfs; a rollback to a chosen snapshot is a manual action through snapper
Backups use borgbackup, to a local repository or a remote one over sshfs
Home Assistant runs as a podman container pulled from registry.freedombox.org; the app text says security, quality and legal reviews are left to upstream and updates follow an independent cycle
Official images cover amd64, arm64, armhf and i386 plus named boards including Raspberry Pi 2, 3 and 4, Rock64, RockPro64 and Pine A64; Raspberry Pi 5 is not listed
